neighbors.heading: no one would choose it
neighbors.text: Today God looked at the man by himself and said, not good. A philosopher reached the same place by watching people. Aristotle wrote that we are social by nature, and about friends he was blunt: "without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods." A full house and a full purse, with no one to share them, isn't a good life.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, God sees the loneliness and makes a partner who fits. Aristotle needs no garden and no God here: he reasons from human nature that we're made to live among others, and that we grow good friendships ourselves.
neighbors.shared: nobody is meant to carry a life alone.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (W. D. Ross translation, 1908); Politics I.2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a friend, or death
neighbors.text: Today's "not good" is a Jewish verse too, and the rabbis kept its lesson alive. The Talmud tells of Honi, who slept for seventy years. He woke, and no one in the study hall knew him or believed who he was. Heartbroken, he prayed to die. The rabbis drew one saying from it: either companionship or death.
neighbors.difference: Christians often hear the garden story through Jesus, who quoted it about marriage. Jewish teachers carried it into learning as well: Torah is often studied in pairs, with a chavruta, a partner who argues with you and keeps you company.
neighbors.shared: we all need someone who knows our name.

neighbors.heading: a fish's warning
neighbors.text: Today the waters rose and God shut Noah in. An old Hindu text tells of a flood too. Manu, an ancestor of humankind, saves a tiny fish, and the fish warns him: a flood is coming, build a ship. When the waters rise, Manu ties his ship to the fish's horn and is pulled to a northern mountain. Later Hindu stories say the fish was Vishnu himself.
neighbors.difference: Genesis gives a reason: the earth was full of violence, and God saves Noah's family and the animals. The Brahmana gives no reason, and Manu survives alone; a new humanity begins from him and his offering.
neighbors.shared: in the deepest water, someone is still looking out for you.

neighbors.heading: in god's name, sail
neighbors.text: Today the fountains of the deep broke open. Muslims tell the flood too, with Noah, Nuh, as a prophet who warned his people for years. When the ark is ready, the Qur'an gives his words: "Embark therein! In the name of Allah be its course and its mooring." Muslims say bismillah, in the name of God, at the start of things.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, Noah's whole family boards. In the Qur'an, one of Nuh's sons refuses, saying he'll climb a mountain, and is lost in the waves while his father calls to him: grief inside the rescue.
neighbors.shared: begin the hard journey with god's name on your lips.

neighbors.heading: every guest as christ
neighbors.text: Today Abraham ran to feed three strangers. Catholic monks turned that run into a rule. Saint Benedict told his monks to welcome every guest as Christ himself, because Christ will say, I was a stranger and you took me in. The abbot was to pour water on the guests' hands, and the whole community was to wash their feet.
neighbors.difference: Every Christian can read Mamre as a call to welcome. Catholic religious life built it into the daily rule of the monastery, so a guest house and a greeting at the door became part of how monks pray.
neighbors.shared: the stranger at your door deserves your best bread.
neighbors.sources: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 53 (paraphrase); Matthew 25:35

neighbors.heading: the true bargain
neighbors.text: Today a morsel of bread became a feast for strangers. Sikhs tell a story of young Guru Nanak. His father gave him money to make a good deal at the market. On the way he met hungry holy men and spent it all feeding them. That, he said, was the true bargain. Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen open to anyone.
neighbors.difference: Abraham's guests turn out to be messengers bringing God's promise. In langar, no one asks who you are: everyone sits side by side on the floor and eats the same food, whatever their caste or creed.
neighbors.shared: whoever comes hungry, there's a place for them.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition, the sacha sauda story (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the place
neighbors.text: Today Jacob woke and said: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Jewish teachers noticed the word place. The rabbis call God HaMakom, the Place, because he is the place of the world, and the world is not his place. Jews still use that name when they comfort mourners.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus pick up Jacob's ladder: he told Nathanael he'd see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Jewish readers have their own readings; one finds God present wherever a person wakes.
neighbors.shared: the ordinary ground under you can be holy.

neighbors.heading: a jewel in your coat
neighbors.text: Today Jacob found God had been there all along, and he hadn't known. The Lotus Sutra tells of a poor man whose friend sewed a priceless jewel into his coat while he slept. He wandered for years, scraping by, never knowing. When they met again, the friend showed him: you were rich the whole time.
neighbors.difference: Jacob discovers God present in a place. In the Lotus Sutra, the jewel stands for the awakening the Buddha planted in his followers long before; Buddhists don't speak of a creator God here.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for may already be right here.
neighbors.sources: Lotus Sutra, chapter 8, the parable of the jewel in the robe (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a word in the pit
neighbors.text: Today Joseph was thrown into a dry pit. Muslims know this story well: Yusuf has a whole surah of the Qur'an. And there, in the pit, Allah speaks to him: "Thou wilt tell them of this deed of theirs when they know (thee) not." His father Yaqub meets the bloodied shirt with "comely patience."
neighbors.difference: Genesis is silent while Joseph is in the pit; God's hand shows only later. In the Qur'an, Allah reassures Yusuf right there in the dark, and Yusuf is honored as a prophet.
neighbors.shared: the pit is not the end of your story.

neighbors.heading: the last freedom
neighbors.text: Today Joseph sat in a pit while his brothers ate lunch. The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl survived Nazi camps and wrote about what can't be taken from a person. Everything else can go, he said, but not the freedom to choose your attitude in any circumstances. People who still had a reason, someone or something waiting, often found a way to endure.
neighbors.difference: Genesis says the Lord was with Joseph and turned the evil toward good. Frankl writes as a doctor: meaning is found by the person, even in suffering, and his claim doesn't depend on God.
neighbors.shared: even at the bottom, something in you is still yours.
neighbors.sources: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: he gave his head
neighbors.text: Today two midwives refused a king's order to kill. Sikhs remember a Guru who refused an emperor. When Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus, were pressed to give up their faith, Guru Tegh Bahadur stood up for them. He was executed in Delhi rather than convert. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, wrote that he gave his head, but not his faith.
neighbors.difference: Shiphrah and Puah live, and God gives them households. Guru Tegh Bahadur was not rescued; Sikhs honor his death for the freedom of people of another religion to keep their own.
neighbors.shared: sometimes faith looks like a quiet, brave no.
neighbors.sources: Bachittar Natak, Guru Gobind Singh (paraphrase); Sikh historical tradition

neighbors.heading: the boy who wouldn't stop
neighbors.text: Today two women feared God more than Pharaoh. Hindus tell of Prahlada, whose father, the demon king Hiranyakashipu, demanded to be worshipped. Prahlada kept praying to Vishnu. His father threatened him again and again, and still the boy wouldn't stop. In the end Vishnu burst from a pillar as Narasimha, half man, half lion, to save him.
neighbors.difference: The midwives are saved by a quick answer and quiet courage; God's reward comes after. Prahlada is saved by Vishnu appearing in person, in a form that slipped past every protection his father had.
neighbors.shared: no king's order outranks what's right.

neighbors.heading: drop by drop
neighbors.text: Today Pharaoh hardened his heart, then did it again, and again. The Buddha described that slow build: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little." The next verse says the same of good: the wise fill up with it, drop by drop.
neighbors.difference: Exodus says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, and later that the LORD hardened it, which readers still wrestle with. In Buddhist teaching no God hardens anyone; our own repeated actions shape the mind.
neighbors.shared: small choices, repeated, become who we are.

neighbors.heading: how habits harden
neighbors.text: Today relief came, and Pharaoh took his word back, again and again. The Catholic Church names this pattern plainly. Its Catechism teaches that sin creates a pull toward more sin: repeat the same act, and it becomes a vice, clouding the conscience until right and wrong are harder to see.
neighbors.difference: Catholics also name a cure: confession, a sacrament where a priest speaks Christ's forgiveness aloud. Many other Christians confess straight to God, without a priest.
neighbors.shared: a hard heart can still be softened.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1865 (paraphrase); Exodus 8:15

neighbors.heading: rich in what you let alone
neighbors.text: Today the manna rotted when people hoarded it. Henry David Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond to find out how little he truly needed. He came back with this: "a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone." Enough isn't a pile. It's a way of seeing.
neighbors.difference: Manna is a gift from God, gathered fresh each morning in trust. Thoreau's simplicity is a choice a person makes with clear eyes, an experiment in living, without needing anyone to send the bread.
neighbors.shared: enough for today can be enough.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

neighbors.heading: two loaves
neighbors.text: Today God sent bread for one day at a time. Jews remember it every week. Before the sabbath, a double portion fell, so on Shabbat two loaves of challah sit on the table. And the Talmud warns: whoever has bread in the basket and asks, what will I eat tomorrow, is of little faith.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear manna in "give us this day our daily bread," and in Jesus calling himself the bread of life. Jews keep it at their own table, in two loaves under a cloth each Shabbat.
neighbors.shared: trust shows up in how we think about tomorrow's bread.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 16:22; Talmud, Shabbat 117b and Sotah 48b (paraphrase); Matthew 6:11; John 6:35

neighbors.heading: the great vow
neighbors.text: Today God gave short, blunt rules: don't kill, don't steal, don't lie. Hindus know a short list too. In the Yoga Sutras, Patanjali names five restraints: non-harming, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint, and not grasping. He calls them a great vow, for everyone, no matter their birth, place or time.
neighbors.difference: At Sinai the commandments are God's words in a covenant with a people. Patanjali's restraints are the first step of a yoga path toward a still, clear mind, held as dharma rather than tablets from a mountain.
neighbors.shared: a good life starts with a few simple don'ts.

neighbors.heading: kindness to parents
neighbors.text: Today the second tablet began at home: honor your father and mother. The Qur'an has its own list, and parents come right after God: "Thy Lord hath decreed, that ye worship none save Him, and (that ye show) kindness to parents." The verses go on: don't kill, don't go near adultery, don't touch an orphan's wealth, give full measure.
neighbors.difference: Christians receive the ten words through Moses and hear Jesus sum them up in love of God and neighbor. Muslims receive this list as revelation to Muhammad, part of the Qur'an recited in prayer.
neighbors.shared: honoring your parents is where goodness learns to walk.

neighbors.heading: theirs, not ours
neighbors.text: Today the farmer left the corners of the field for the poor. Catholics keep a line from Pope Saint Gregory the Great: when we give the poor what they need, we aren't handing over what is ours. We're giving back what is theirs. The Church teaches that the goods of the earth are meant for everyone.
neighbors.difference: Catholic teaching gathers this into a long tradition of social teaching from popes and bishops. Other Christians often speak of stewardship and generosity, without one shared body of teaching.
neighbors.shared: some of what you hold was always meant for someone else.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2402 and 2446, quoting Gregory the Great (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: work, then share
neighbors.text: Today the edges of the harvest belonged to the poor. Sikhs are taught to work honestly and share what they earn. Guru Nanak said it in one line: one who eats what he earns by his own work, and gives some of it away, knows the path. Many Sikhs set aside a tenth, dasvandh, for others.
neighbors.difference: Leviticus leaves food in the field for the poor to gather themselves. Sikhs also share it cooked and served: at langar, anyone sits on the floor and eats as an equal.
neighbors.shared: honest work is made whole by sharing it.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak, Var Sarang, Ang 1245 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: more roots than branches
neighbors.text: Today's psalm pictured a person like a tree by rivers of water. The Mishnah grew that tree further. A person whose learning is greater than their deeds is like a tree with many branches and few roots: the wind tips it over. One whose deeds are greater is like a tree with deep roots: every wind in the world can't move it.
neighbors.difference: Christians often read Psalm 1 alongside Jesus' house built on rock. The Mishnah's sage measures it his own way: branches are what you know, roots are what you do, and the roots must win.
neighbors.shared: what you do sinks deeper roots than what you know.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (3:22 in some editions) (paraphrase); Jeremiah 17:8; Matthew 7:24

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today's psalm warned about where you walk, stand and sit, and with whom. Buddhists tell of Ananda, who said to the Buddha: good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrected him. Don't say that, he said. Good friends, good companions, are the whole of it.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's happy person delights in God's law day and night. In the Buddha's teaching, a good friend helps you walk the path to freedom from suffering, with no creator God in view.
neighbors.shared: the company you keep shapes what you grow into.

neighbors.heading: don't despair
neighbors.text: Today David's silence dried him out until he told God everything. Muslims turn back too; it's called tawbah, returning. The Qur'an speaks to anyone who has gone wrong: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins."
neighbors.difference: Christians hear forgiveness in Psalm 32 and see it fulfilled through Jesus' cross. Muslims turn to Allah directly, with no one between, and the Qur'an says Allah can even change bad deeds into good ones for those who repent.
neighbors.shared: it's never too late to come back.

neighbors.heading: the weight of a secret
neighbors.text: Today the psalm said that holding a wrong inside made the bones ache. Psychologists have studied that weight. James Pennebaker asked people to write about painful things they'd kept to themselves. In his studies, many felt better afterward, and some even needed the doctor less. Putting it into words seemed to set something down.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's relief comes from God, who forgives. Psychology describes the relief of telling, and says nothing about who, if anyone, forgives.
neighbors.shared: what we stop hiding stops weighing us down.
neighbors.sources: James W. Pennebaker, research on expressive writing (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the fish and the water
neighbors.text: Today the psalm longed for God like a deer for water. Guru Nanak used water too. He told his own mind: love the Lord the way a fish loves water. The more water there is, the happier the fish; take it away, and it can't live a moment.
neighbors.difference: The psalmist thirsts from far away, cast down, remembering the temple. For Guru Nanak, the water is the Name, and the longing is met by remembering it, day after day, wherever you are.
neighbors.shared: some thirst is a sign of where we belong.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: like a calf for milk
neighbors.text: Today a deer panted for running water. In a Hindu scripture, a dying warrior named Vritra prays the same ache to Vishnu: like baby birds without wings longing for their mother, like a hungry calf longing for milk, like a lover longing for the beloved far away, so my mind longs to see you, lotus-eyed one.
neighbors.difference: The psalmist longs for the one God of Israel, whom Christians know in Jesus. Vritra longs for Vishnu, seen with lotus eyes; for many Hindus, the one divine is loved in such personal forms.
neighbors.shared: longing for god is a kind of prayer.

items.lessonTitle: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 90)

neighbors.heading: five things to remember
neighbors.text: Today the psalm asked God to teach us to count our days. The Buddha gave five things to remember often: I will grow old. I will get sick. I will die. Everything I love will change, and I will be parted from it. And my actions are what I truly own.
neighbors.difference: The psalm counts our days so God can give us a heart of wisdom and satisfy us with mercy. The Buddha's reflection is meant to loosen clinging and turn us to good action, with no creator asked to help.
neighbors.shared: remembering life is short helps us live it well.

neighbors.heading: dust thou art
neighbors.text: Today the psalm said our lives are like grass. Catholics feel that on their foreheads each Ash Wednesday, when ashes are marked and words from Genesis can be spoken: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." Saint Benedict told his monks to keep death daily before their eyes, so each day would count.
neighbors.difference: Ash Wednesday is kept by Catholics and some other churches. For Catholics the ashes are a sacramental, a blessed sign that opens Lent, while many Christians mark the season without them.
neighbors.shared: counting our days makes each one matter.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 3:19 (Douay-Rheims); Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 4 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: name it to tame it
neighbors.text: Today exiles hung their harps on the willows, and the psalm kept even their rage. Psychologists have noticed that naming a hard feeling can loosen its grip. In Matthew Lieberman's brain studies, putting feelings into words calmed the brain's alarm center. The psalm said its grief out loud instead of performing a happy song.
neighbors.difference: The psalm speaks its grief and anger to God, and readers still struggle with its last lines. Psychology says nothing about who hears; it only finds that naming the feeling helps.
neighbors.shared: sorrow said honestly is easier to carry.
neighbors.sources: Matthew D. Lieberman and colleagues, research on affect labeling (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the broken glass
neighbors.text: Today the exiles vowed: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Jews still keep that vow. At Jewish weddings, at the height of joy, a glass is broken to remember Jerusalem, and sometimes this very verse is said. Jews pray facing toward Jerusalem, too.
neighbors.difference: Christians often read Jerusalem in the psalm as also the heavenly city, the home Jesus promised. For Jews it is also a real city on a real hill, remembered at weddings and in prayers facing it.
neighbors.shared: even our happiest days can hold room for remembering.

neighbors.heading: the king who kept his word
neighbors.text: Today Job lost everything and still did not curse God. Hindus tell of King Harishchandra, tested by the sage Vishvamitra. To keep a promise, he gave up his kingdom, then was parted from his wife and son, and worked guarding a cremation ground. Through every loss, he would not break his word.
neighbors.difference: Job is tested on whether he'll serve God for nothing. Harishchandra is tested on truth, keeping his word whatever it costs, and in the end the gods restore him for it.
neighbors.shared: goodness that holds when everything's lost is goodness indeed.
neighbors.sources: Markandeya Purana, the story of Harishchandra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: most merciful
neighbors.text: Today Job sat in the ashes. Muslims know him as the prophet Ayyub. The Qur'an gives his prayer: "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." He doesn't demand; he names the pain and names God's mercy. Allah answers, restores him, and says: "Lo! We found him steadfast."
neighbors.difference: The book of Job is long, with friends who argue and a whirlwind that answers. The Qur'an tells Ayyub's story in a few verses and holds him up as a model of patience, sabr.
neighbors.shared: you can tell god it hurts and still trust his mercy.

neighbors.heading: idleness, the enemy
neighbors.text: Today the ant worked with no boss. Saint Benedict wrote in his rule for monks that idleness is the enemy of the soul, so the brothers should spend set hours working with their hands and set hours in holy reading. They are truly monks, he said, when they live by the labor of their hands.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians speak of work as a calling from God. Catholic tradition also sets work inside the rhythm of prayer in its monasteries, and keeps a feast for Saint Joseph the Worker, a carpenter.
neighbors.shared: honest work can be a way of prayer.

neighbors.heading: the carpenter's bread
neighbors.text: Today the ant gathered food in summer. Sikhs tell a story of Guru Nanak in a town called Saidpur. A rich official invited him to a feast; he chose instead to eat with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter. Pressed to explain, the story says, he squeezed the two breads: from Lalo's came milk, from the rich man's, blood.
neighbors.difference: Proverbs praises the ant for working ahead and storing up. Sikhs honor kirat karni, honest work, above all for how it's earned: cleanly, without exploiting anyone, and then shared.
neighbors.shared: bread earned honestly feeds more than the body.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition, Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the first words awake
neighbors.text: Today the poet found God's mercies "new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Many Jews say those last words each morning. Before getting out of bed, eyes barely open, they say Modeh Ani: I thank you, living King, for returning my soul to me with compassion; great is your faithfulness.
neighbors.difference: Christians sing this verse in hymns and hear God's faithfulness fulfilled in Jesus. Jews carry it into the first breath of the day, thanking God for the soul given back after sleep.
neighbors.shared: every morning is a gift handed back to you.
neighbors.sources: Lamentations 3:23; Modeh Ani, the Jewish waking prayer (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: only today
neighbors.text: Today mercy came new each morning, not stored up from yesterday. The Buddha taught a short verse about this one day: don't chase the past, don't lose yourself in the future. The past is gone, the future hasn't come. See what is here, now, clearly, and do today what needs doing.
neighbors.difference: Lamentations rests on God's steady love, renewed each dawn. The Buddha points to the present moment itself, and Buddhists don't look to a creator to renew it.
neighbors.shared: this morning is a fresh place to begin.

neighbors.heading: if they lean toward peace
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah saw swords beaten into plowshares. The Qur'an calls paradise the home of peace: "Allah summoneth to the abode of peace." And facing an enemy, it says: "And if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it, and trust in Allah." Muslims greet each other with peace: as-salamu alaykum.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah sees a day when nations stop learning war. The Qur'an also sets rules for when fighting is allowed, and tells believers to choose peace whenever the other side reaches for it.
neighbors.shared: when someone reaches for peace, reach back.

neighbors.heading: a peace people build
neighbors.text: Today the iron that killed was reforged to feed. The philosopher Immanuel Kant wrote a short book called Perpetual Peace. He argued that lasting peace isn't just a dream: nations could build it, with fair laws at home, a federation of free states, and, in time, an end to standing armies.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah's peace comes when the nations go up to God's mountain to learn his ways. Kant's peace is built by people through reason and agreements, without needing a mountain or a prophet.
neighbors.shared: you can turn what wounds into something that feeds.

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today God promised to write his law on the heart. Guru Tegh Bahadur asked a gentle question in one of his hymns: why go searching for God in the forest? He lives in everything, always untouched, and he's already with you. Like fragrance in a flower, like a reflection in a mirror, he is within.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah promises a new covenant on a day to come, which Christians see begun in Jesus. Guru Tegh Bahadur says the Lord is within already; the work is to look, and to remember the Name.
neighbors.shared: what matters most is closer than you think.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Raag Dhanasari, Ang 684 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seated in every heart
neighbors.text: Today the law moved from stone to the heart. Near the end of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, moving them all. Then he says: take refuge in him with your whole being, and by his grace you will find peace.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah's promise is a covenant, God writing his teaching on a people's heart. In the Gita, the Lord is already seated within every living being; Hindu schools read that as oneness or as close belonging.
neighbors.shared: the truest teacher may be speaking from inside you.

neighbors.heading: as a mother protects
neighbors.text: Today God held a toddler's arms and bent down to feed him. In a Buddhist teaching on loving-kindness, the Buddha reaches for a parent too: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let a person grow a boundless love for every living being.
neighbors.difference: In Hosea, the parent's love comes from God toward his people. In the Metta Sutta, that mother's love is something a person grows in themselves, toward all beings; no God is needed.
neighbors.shared: the best love looks like a parent's care.

neighbors.heading: father, and mother too
neighbors.text: Today God was a parent bending down to feed a child. The Catholic Catechism says God's tenderness can also be pictured as a mother's, though God is beyond both. The English mystic Julian of Norwich, honored by Catholics, wrote it boldly: as truly as God is our Father, so truly is God our Mother.
neighbors.difference: Catholics, like Orthodox Christians, see a mother's care in Mary and ask her prayers; she is not God, but the Church calls her mother. Many other Christians honor Mary without asking her prayers.
neighbors.shared: you were held before you ever noticed.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 239 (paraphrase); Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, chapter 59 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one word for a life
neighbors.text: Today Micah boiled everything down to three: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Confucius was once asked for one word to guide a whole life. He answered: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others."
neighbors.difference: Micah's three end with walking humbly with God. Confucius keeps his rule among people, at home and in the town; he spoke little of spirits, and his guide works whether or not you pray.
neighbors.shared: a whole good life can fit in one short line.

neighbors.heading: 613, then three
neighbors.text: Today Micah gave a short answer to a big question. The Talmud noticed. It says Moses received 613 commandments, then prophets came and gathered them into fewer: David into eleven, Isaiah into six, and Micah into three: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God.
neighbors.difference: Christians often read Micah 6:8 as a life lived by grace in Christ. In the Talmud, the short lists don't replace the 613; they show the heart of commandments Jews still keep.
neighbors.shared: underneath many rules, a few simple loves.

neighbors.heading: steady in gain and loss
neighbors.text: Today Habakkuk lost figs, grapes, olives, grain and flocks, and still said yet. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to do his work without clinging to how it turns out, the same in success and failure. That evenness of mind, he says, is what yoga is.
neighbors.difference: Krishna teaches a mind that stays steady, unmoved by gain or loss. Habakkuk isn't unmoved: he trembles first, then chooses joy in God anyway, while the loss is still real.
neighbors.shared: peace can stand even when the fields are bare.

neighbors.heading: good either way
neighbors.text: Today Habakkuk rejoiced beside empty stalls. The Prophet Muhammad said something like it: how wonderful is the believer's affair, for all of it is good. If something good comes, he is grateful, and that is good for him. If hardship comes, he is patient, and that is good for him too.
neighbors.difference: Habakkuk speaks from one terrible season, choosing joy in God. The hadith covers both kinds of days and names two answers, gratitude and patience, shukr and sabr.
neighbors.shared: there's a way to stay grateful whatever the harvest.

neighbors.heading: oil for the sick
neighbors.text: Today Jeremiah asked why there was no healing balm. Catholics answer with oil. The letter of James says: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." The Church keeps it as a sacrament, the Anointing of the Sick.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians pray for the sick, and some anoint them. For Catholics this anointing is one of seven sacraments, given by a priest, and they believe Christ himself acts in it to strengthen and heal.
neighbors.shared: no one should face sickness without someone at their side.
neighbors.sources: James 5:14 (Douay-Rheims); Catechism of the Catholic Church 1499–1532 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the medicine of the name
neighbors.text: Today the weeping prophet asked: is there no physician there? Sikhs have a line about medicine in Sukhmani Sahib, a long hymn of peace by Guru Arjan: the Name of God is the medicine for every illness. Many Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib when someone is ill or grieving.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah weeps because the medicine is there and his people aren't healed. For Sikhs, the medicine is remembering the Name, and it's always within reach, whoever you are.
neighbors.shared: there is a balm, even when it's hard to find.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Now let me go in peace (Luke 2:21–35)

neighbors.heading: into his hand
neighbors.text: Today old Simeon held a baby and said he could now go in peace. Jews sing a hymn called Adon Olam, often at the end of prayers and at bedtime. Its last lines put the soul in God's hands: into his hand I place my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake. The LORD is with me; I will not fear.
neighbors.difference: Christians believe Simeon saw the Messiah he'd waited for, in the child Jesus. Judaism still looks ahead to the messianic age, and Jews sing Adon Olam's trust in God in the meantime.
neighbors.shared: you can rest when you know whose hands hold you.
neighbors.sources: Adon Olam, closing lines (paraphrase); Psalm 31:6 (31:5 in KJV)

neighbors.heading: a peaceful last word
neighbors.text: Today Simeon was ready to be relieved of his watch. The Buddha, lying down for the last time at Kusinara, was calm, and his last words were for his students: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
neighbors.difference: Simeon's peace comes from seeing the promised child, the salvation God sent. The Buddha's peace comes from seeing that everything changes, and he hands the work to his students rather than to a savior.
neighbors.shared: a life lived well can end in peace.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 16, Maha-parinibbana Sutta, chapter 6 (Rhys Davids)

neighbors.heading: give full measure
neighbors.text: Today John told tax collectors not to cheat and soldiers not to extort. A surah of the Qur'an opens: "Woe unto the defrauders," those who demand full measure for themselves and short-weigh others. And Muslims give zakat, a set share of their wealth each year, for those in need.
neighbors.difference: John gives each crowd a simple, personal answer as they turn back to God. In Islam, zakat is one of the five pillars, a required act of worship with its own fixed share.
neighbors.shared: fair weights and open hands go together.

neighbors.heading: the child in the pond
neighbors.text: Today John said: if you have two coats, give one away. The philosopher Peter Singer asks you to picture a child drowning in a shallow pond. You'd wade in, even if it ruined your shoes. Then he asks: if you can prevent something bad without giving up anything as important, shouldn't you, near or far?
neighbors.difference: John calls people to turn toward God before the one who is coming. Singer argues from reason alone, without appeal to God: there's the person in need, and your coat.
neighbors.shared: if you have more than enough, someone's need is close.
